summary: Describes Public 4over6, a mechanism for giving IPv4 Internet connectivity over an IPv6 access network using global IPv4 addresses and IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels, in a hub-and-spoke model. It is in use in places but not recommended for new deployments, where Lightweight 4over6 should be used.

plainLanguage.summary: Old-style letters are put inside new-style envelopes so they can travel along the new roads.

questions: how does ipv4 over ipv6 tunneling work
subtitle: Giving users a real, unshared IPv4 address through an IPv6-only access network by tunneling IPv4 inside IPv6.

tldr.problem: Operators moving to an IPv6-only access network must still give users IPv4 connectivity, ideally with a full global IPv4 address and no address translation.
tldr.mechanism: Each customer device (CE) gets a global IPv4 address and a stateful IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel to a border relay (BR), which keeps a binding table between each CE's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: It is in active deployment in some environments, but the RFC says it is not recommended for new deployments, which should use Lightweight 4over6.

today: RFC 7040 is an Informational document from November 2013, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says Public 4over6 is not recommended for new deployments and that future ones should use Lightweight 4over6.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Operators moving to an IPv6-only access network still need to give users IPv4 connectivity to reach the IPv4-only Internet. Public 4over6 does this with IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels as defined in RFC 2473, following the Hub and Spoke softwire model of RFC 4925. The ISP can then run an IPv6-only infrastructure and avoid spreading scarce IPv4 addresses through the network.

The aims are end-to-end transparency and flexibility. Users get global, non-shared IPv4 addresses, so neither carrier-side nor user-side translation is needed. That matters for protocols other than TCP and UDP (such as IPsec and L2TP) and for well-known ports (such as HTTP and SMTP). IPv4 and IPv6 address plans are independent, since the user's IPv4 address is not embedded in the IPv6 address. The price is that the tunnel concentrator must keep per-subscriber binding state.

The RFC says Public 4over6 is in active deployment in some environments, in particular China Next Generation Internet (CNGI) and China Education and Research Network 2 (CERNET2), but is not recommended for new deployments. Future deployments should use Lightweight 4over6.
sections.plainLanguage: The new roads only carry new-style traffic. This puts old-style traffic in new-style envelopes, and every customer keeps their own full old-style address.

sections.title: Elements and Use Cases
sections.content:
Two roles are defined. A 4over6 Customer Edge (CE) is either a dual-stack host with an IPv6-only uplink or a dual-stack CPE, and it has a tunnel interface for IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation. A 4over6 Border Relay (BR) is a dual-stack router at the edge of the operator's IPv6 access network that terminates the tunnels and connects to the IPv4 Internet. The BR can also act as a DHCPv4-over-IPv6 server or relay.

An ISP with plenty of global IPv4 addresses can offer Public 4over6 to all customers. An ISP short of addresses can use Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) as the basic service and offer Public 4over6 as a value-added service that avoids the degradation caused by the Carrier Grade NAT. An IPv4 application server is a typical high-end user: it can register DNS directly with a dedicated address and needs no NAT traversal for incoming traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer's box is the front door, and the border relay is the post office that unwraps the envelopes. The post office knows which house goes with which address.

sections.title: Provisioning an IPv4 Address
sections.content:
First the CE gets an IPv6 address or prefix and learns the BR's IPv6 address, using DHCPv6 or other means, and configures its WAN interface. Then it gets a public IPv4 address by DHCPv4 over IPv6 or by static configuration, and configures its tunnel interface. The BR learns the CE's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses from information provided by the DHCPv4 server and updates its IPv4-IPv6 binding table.

Usually each CE gets one global IPv4 address, though a CE may need a prefix. Static configuration suits application servers, which need a stable address, and enterprise networks, which usually need a prefix because DHCPv4 does not support prefix allocation. In that case the user and ISP negotiate the addresses beforehand and each configures its own side.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer's box first learns its new-road address and where the post office is. Then it asks for its old-style address, and the post office writes the pair in its book.

sections.title: CE and BR Behavior
sections.content:
The CE encapsulates outgoing IPv4 packets using the BR's IPv6 address as destination and its own IPv6 address as source. On receipt it removes the IPv6 header and either delivers locally or forwards by the IPv4 destination. With a single IPv4 address, the CE runs regular NAPT for its customer network, with the tunnel address as the external address. With a prefix, NAPT is not necessary. A CE can fall back to Dual-Stack Lite if it cannot get a global IPv4 address.

The BR keeps the bindings between each CE's IPv6 and IPv4 addresses. It installs a binding when it sends a DHCP ACK and deletes it when the lease expires or a RELEASE arrives, either as the DHCP server itself or by snooping as a relay. For packets from a CE, it checks the inner IPv4 source against the outer IPv6 source in the binding table and silently drops the packet if there is no match. For packets toward a CE, it looks up the IPv4 destination to find the IPv6 destination and encapsulates with its own IPv6 address as source. It also supports hairpinning of traffic between two CEs.

Fragmentation, reassembly and DNS handling follow the corresponding sections of RFC 6333.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office checks that every envelope comes from the address the book says it should. If the pair is not in the book, the envelope is thrown away quietly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The BR must limit service to registered customers. On the control plane it allocates IPv4 addresses only to registered customers, for example by responding only to DHCP requests from registered IPv6 source addresses. This does not work with multi-homing, so multi-homing is disallowed in networks where Public 4over6 is deployed. Alternatively, the BR can filter unregistered CE requests during the DHCP process.

For data packets, the BR performs ingress filtering with the binding table. If a CE falls back to DS-Lite, the security considerations of RFC 6333 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people on the guest list get an address, and the post office checks the guest list on every envelope.
